newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African policeman tells of secret strategy.
newsitem.headline: S.African policeman tells of secret strategy.

text.p: An apartheid-era police captain and convicted murderer gave fresh details on Tuesday of how white South African governments took sides in inter-black rivalry to fight the African National Congress.
Brian Mitchell, sentenced to death in 1992 for killing 11 blacks in a massacre in KwaZulu-Natal province in 1988, is seeking amnesty from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

His written submission to the commission echoed evidence in the murder trial of former defence minister Magnus Malan to the effect that apartheid governments backed the Inkatha Freedom Party in its violent feud with President Nelson Mandela's ANC.

Malan and his 19 co-accused were all acquitted last week of a 1987 massacre in which 13 blacks died. The judge said evidence against them was inadequate but added that the murders were almost certainly carried out by Inkatha members.

Mitchell, whose sentence was commuted to 30 years in jail, said Inkatha members were trained as "special constables" by the apartheid government to combat the then-banned ANC and the allied United Democratic Front (UDF).
"Everything boiled down to an undeclared civil war between Inkatha-government-security forces and the ANC backed by the UDF," he said in his amnesty application.
"The security forces sided with Inkatha and this kept the focus away from the whites; violence would appear to be black on black," Mitchell said.
Mitchell is the first apartheid-era policeman to appear before the amnesty committee of the truth commission chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
He was convicted of having ordered six of the special constables to carry out the 1988 attack in Trust Feed, a black settlement near Pietermaritzburg.
Mitchell said speeches by the then-president P.W. Botha and his defence minister Malan had demonised the ANC and strengthened his resolve to prevent it from gaining strongholds in KwaZulu-Natal.
The government set up joint management committees between the police and the South African Defence Force (SADF) to wage counter revolutionary warfare against the ANC, he said.
"It has by now become clear to me that the SADF generals were effectively running the country at that point of our history," Mitchell said.

The truth commission can grant amnesty to perpetrators of human rights abuses from across the political spectrum if it believes they have made full and honest confessions and that their crimes were politically motivated.
